decisions.rationale: The anchor owns stage and unstage index mutation semantics. The nearby comparator features concern catalog reconciliation, generic hunk launch policy, mixed diff/unstage/discard wiring, discard-only destruction, or accessibility; none has the same operation set and failure boundary.

PF-0017 describes the same worktree UI command catalog authority, registrations, compatibility normalization, arguments, outcomes, and production-wiring incompleteness. Binding actions, mock lineage, and settings controls are consumers or adjacent surfaces rather than the catalog itself.

The anchor is specifically the prune, release, and remove destructive lifecycle. Comparators either combine removal with merge, aggregate runtime recovery, describe the worktree UI, combine binding transitions, or inventory merge/worktree controls, so they differ in lifecycle and state boundary.

PF-0110 includes pinned-workflow lifecycle but also Actions information architecture and replay. That umbrella/member relationship does not equal the anchor's isolated authoritative persistence and scope question for pin state.

The anchor governs initial local project and remote repository creation, including duplicate races and rollback. The closest comparators define general GitHub authority boundaries or later optional promotion and attachment handoffs, which have different initiation, state, and partial-outcome semantics.

Run-start worktree/Git configuration projection is not the shared project-context propagation feature or the cleanup module's configuration policy. Those comparators share configuration vocabulary but have different authorities, consumers, and failure outcomes.

The anchor isolates durable worktree-conflict lineage across restart and reconciliation. The comparators cover merge/removal gates, a broad runtime-recovery umbrella, generic file-operation conflict sessions, or UI control lifecycle, none of which shares that persistence boundary.

The anchor owns the centralized worktree lifecycle and canonical branch identity. Comparator features cover allocation-name races, broad runtime recovery, user binding actions, or branch/merge policy; they are dependent members or adjacent transitions, not the same authority and lifecycle.

The anchor is the durable allocation and fenced-lease system for lanes and worktrees. Package-aware projections, runtime recovery, owner-routing boundaries, and workspace cleanup consume or constrain it but do not share its lease state machine or failure semantics.

No comparator owns Git binary resolution plus locale-independent subprocess classification, retry accounting, cleanup, and repository/index race protection. The cited neighbors only establish broad Git boundaries or expose authority-unbound Git controls.

No comparator defines repository-scoped Doctor mutation authority or its fail-closed ambient-directory rule. The Source Control recovery CTA is only a display and navigation seam, so it is related recovery UX but has different authority and outcome.

The anchor establishes requested/effective remote-versus-local worktree identity authority. Handoff staleness, frozen cwd launch, executor binding validation, and remote reconnect/path safety are downstream lifecycle checks rather than the same identity-owner contract.

The anchor specifically governs startup membership revalidation and failure classification. Handoff staleness, creation identity allocation, and execution-time binding validation occur at different lifecycle boundaries and yield different recovery actions.

The anchor is a cross-operation safety aggregate for merge, rebase, push, pull requests, branches, locks, and recovery. Each comparator covers only a member operation, a broader surface, or an ownership seam; strict umbrella/member exclusion prevents a merge.

The anchor combines shell-owned PTY sessions with command cards, review/search, attach, workspace fidelity, and recovery. Comparator features address owner completeness, tab identity, missing terminal sections, or byte-stream delivery, each with a narrower or different state boundary.

The anchor owns dev-intent-to-PTY handoff, attributed shell evidence, and close or switch retention consequences. General terminal coherence, adjunct-session secure restore, and missing terminal surface recovery do not produce the same handoff lifecycle or user outcome.

The anchor jointly preserves the distinction between whole-turn multi-file revert and conversation rewind while defining transaction safety. Resend history loss, bounded undo scope, restore-event delivery, and exact single-revert identity are related members with different authorities and failure boundaries.

The anchor is the complete Assistant worktree scope across UI, lifecycle, settings, events, commands, and errors. Comparators are component catalogs, recovery subsets, UI subsets, binding actions, or non-authoritative mock lineage; none equals the full scoped product boundary.

The anchor is the exact Assistant-consumer versus Source-Control-layout ownership seam. Comparator owner maps separate other surfaces or Orchestrator concerns, describe broader owner/consumer reconciliation, or classify mock lineage, so their authorities and outcomes differ.

No comparator defines the per-project persisted Worktrees filter together with fixed section, scroll, isolation, and nesting state. The general Source Control surface and worktree UI contracts are umbrellas with different state coverage.

No comparator specifies the Assistant header Worktree button's exact placement, mode invariance, and no-repository disappearance rule. Worktree binding actions are the button's downstream behavior, not the placement surface.

The anchor is the durable thread-keyed binding record schema. Stale handoff, runtime recovery, execution validation, and user binding actions consume or mutate that record but do not share its storage lifecycle and authority.

The anchor defines repo/worktree/relative-path identity and turn-start freezing for file pivots and historical evidence. Launch cwd guards, executor context, ordinary-tab binding, and compare identity are related consumers or specialized surfaces with different outcomes.

The anchor's user outcome is that mode changes cannot mutate an in-flight turn's worktree and cwd. Comparator features instead validate launch-time cwd or execution context across modes, so their lifecycle boundary and failure semantics differ.

The anchor is the exact create-worktree dialog, fields, defaults, validation, and controls. General worktree UI, combined select/create/unbind actions, and non-authoritative mocks do not share that single dialog state boundary.

The anchor specifies the dialog's success, retryable failure, advisory collision, and loading states. Worktree identity allocation races and combined binding actions influence those states but have different authorities and broader mutation lifecycles.

The anchor's negative capability rule allows user/system creation and removal entrypoints while denying direct AI tool calls. Broad owner maps and concept-lineage classifications do not establish the same caller authority or enforcement outcome.

The anchor is synchronous auto-creation during new-thread dispatch with root fallback and warning. Identity allocation, broad runtime recovery, and manual binding actions are related implementation or user paths, not this lifecycle and outcome.
No comparator isolates title-driven temporary-branch rename failure and its missing event, retry, log, and remediation affordance. Runtime recovery is only a broader neighboring umbrella.

The anchor assigns auto-create runtime ownership, project serialization, atomic reverse writes, and race-only retries. The comparators expose allocation races, broad recovery, or user binding actions without the same owner and retry state machine.

The anchor is exact settings information architecture under Branching with three named groups. General operational worktree UI and settings control inventory do not share the same placement and grouping outcome.

No comparator defines the bound-thread selector glyph, metadata, tooltip, and no-placeholder rule. General transient accessibility and worktree UI contracts are related surface constraints but not the same component state.

The anchor confines keep/remove cleanup to thread deletion and distinguishes unbind from guarded disk prune. Comparator features cover general remove/merge gates, recovery, UI semantics, workspace git-clean policy, or general binding actions, so their triggers and state boundaries differ.

The anchor is the exact thread-delete confirmation presentation, labels, focus, dirty warning, and settings-derived default. Comparator features define broader destructive eligibility or binding transactions without that dialog-specific user outcome.

The anchor is the explicit product decision that forced dirty worktree and branch deletion is irreversible after warning and has no MVP unbind undo. Broader removal gates, UI lifecycle, and binding-action gaps do not encode that same irreversible boundary.

No comparator owns the optional completion toast's trigger, suppression, deduplication, and preference policy. General operational-surface and transient-UI accessibility gaps are related presentation constraints with different outcomes.

The anchor requires four entry paths to equivalent merge and PR outcomes. Source Control operations, surface IA, promotion handoffs, and branch-transition policy are adjacent authorities or execution lifecycles, not the same entrypoint equivalence contract.

No comparator defines Source Control merge routing with thread_id null and intentional omission of thread-only side effects. Executor fallback for absent worktree context is superficially similar null handling but has different authority, risk, and outcome.

The anchor is the exact merge confirmation dialog with strategy, target, conditional message, preserved edits, defaults, and controls. The related comparators define broader safety, worktree UI, or underwired control inventories, not this dialog state.

No comparator isolates cancellation after merge execution begins, including interruption points, cleanup, late success, and resulting modal state. The generic missing merge/worktree lifecycle is a broader neighboring gap.

The anchor is the complete pre-merge fail-closed guard matrix and final binding recheck. PF-0010 combines remove and merge safety and adds confirmation, preservation, and rollback, while other comparators are broader UI/control umbrellas; strict boundaries therefore remain distinct.

The anchor fixes repository execution location by merge strategy. General merge safety gates and underdefined branch/merge transitions affect the same workflow but do not specify the same execution-context outcome.

The anchor owns a project merge lock from guard evaluation through execution and stale-lock recovery. Active-run guards, concurrent confirmation changes, generic lifecycle omissions, and scheduler-limit gaps are adjacent concurrency concerns without the same lock lifecycle.

No comparator defines the canonical squash, merge, and rebase command sequences with worktree_branch aliasing. Generic Source Control execution ownership and branch-transition policy are related but lack the same command-template authority.

The anchor is the explicit non-blocking failed-fetch posture for local pre-merge truth and advisory toast. File Manager offline labeling and remote reconnect security have different owners, state, and mutation consequences.

The anchor draws the exact authority boundary between product non-interactive rebase and terminal-only interactive editing. Broad owner separation and underdefined branch/merge transitions do not encode the same supported-operation boundary.

No comparator isolates mandatory merge-hook rejection, strategy-specific repository residue, retry idempotency, and cleanup. General merge safety, missing control lifecycle, and branch-transition failure policy are broader neighbors.

The anchor is the post-success modal Cancel ambiguity for binding, disk, focus, and repeated prompts. Generic merge/removal safety and lifecycle omissions occur at broader or earlier states and are not equivalent.
